prompt.context: Our client owns a designer shoe-store that makes high end made-to-measure shoes for customers. The high-quality product has gained popularity rapidly and the client wants to ramp up production. However, the highly-skilled labor that our client employs is hard to come by.
prompt.question: Our client wants us to help them figure out how to increase output without adversely affecting quality and the company's potential profitability.

clarifying_info.q: Are there additional skilled shoemakers available to hire?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no additional skilled shoemakers available in the market.

clarifying_info.q: What does the shoe-making process look like?
clarifying_info.a: There are 3 stages: cutting, stitching, and finishing.

clarifying_info.q: How many workers are there and how long does each pair take?
clarifying_info.a: There are 15 workers; each currently takes an average of 12 hours to produce one pair of shoes.

clarifying_info.q: Does each worker perform all steps?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, currently each shoemaker performs all three steps of the process.

clarifying_info.q: Can the process be changed so that shoemakers perform specific tasks?

exhibits.title: Employee Survey
exhibits.shows: A table showing hours per activity for three groups of 5 employees each (Group 1, Group 2, Group 3) across three tasks: Cutting, Stitching, and Finishing. Each group totals 12 hours.

framework: Understand the current production process and identify constraints (skilled labor, no new hires possible)
Analyze existing labor skills and time allocation across process steps
Identify whether task specialization (assembly-line model) can reduce per-unit hours
Quantify output impact: recalculate weekly pairs produced under the new system
Assess profitability: revenue, variable costs (materials, shipping, labor), fixed costs, and net profit
Address risks and implementation steps for the process change

questions.prompt: What is the optimal way to reorganize the workforce to maximize output?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify that each group has one task where it performs at 3 hours (its comparative advantage). Group 1 excels at Cutting (3 hrs), Group 2 excels at Finishing (3 hrs), Group 3 excels at Stitching (3 hrs). By assigning each group to its strongest task, total hours per pair drops from 12 to 9 (3 cutting + 3 stitching + 3 finishing). This is the core insight: specialization, not external hiring or technology, solves the constraint.

questions.prompt: Given the new process, calculate the maximum weekly output and total weekly (and annual) profit.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for price, costs, and hours worked without being prompted. Walk through: (1) output = total available hours / hours per pair; (2) revenue = output x price; (3) subtract variable and fixed costs to get weekly profit; (4) annualize.

math.setup: Employees work 9 hours/day, 5 days/week = 45 hours/week each. 15 employees total. New system: 9 hours/pair. Price $300/pair. Material cost $40/pair, Shipping $10/pair, Employee wages $15/hour, Fixed costs $1,000/week.
steps: Hours per week per employee = 9 hrs/day x 5 days = 45 hrs
Output per employee per week = 45 hrs / 9 hrs per pair = 5 pairs
Total weekly output = 5 pairs x 15 employees = 75 pairs
Materials and delivery cost per pair = $40 + $10 = $50
Total employee cost = 15 employees x 45 hrs x $15/hr = $10,125
math.answer: Weekly output: 75 pairs; Weekly profit: $7,625; Annual profit: $396,500

recommendation: Change the production process to a specialization model: Group 1 handles cutting, Group 2 handles finishing, Group 3 handles stitching — each group performing the task where it takes only 3 hours.

This reduces average production time per pair from 12 hours to 9 hours, increasing weekly output from 62 pairs (current) to 75 pairs without hiring additional workers, generating approximately $396,500 in annual profit.
risks: Employees may resist the change if they are accustomed to the current system, causing friction during transition.
Process changes — especially in entrenched workflows — carry implementation risk; productivity may temporarily dip.
There may be one-time costs associated with reorganizing the workshop layout or retraining workers for their specialized roles.
next_steps: Pilot the specialization model with one group to validate time savings and identify implementation hiccups before rolling out to all 15 workers.
Monitor output and quality metrics closely during the transition period.
Assess whether the workshop layout needs to be reconfigured to support the new flow, and budget for any one-time costs.
